entry.title: How Homebrew Works: The Ruby Architecture Behind brew’s Formula System

link.title: How Homebrew Works: The Ruby Architecture Behind brew’s Formula System

entry.content:
Type brew install ffmpeg on a fresh Mac and Homebrew will resolve, fetch and link a dependency tree that can span dozens of packages — in the right order, without asking you anything, without a lockfile. The order it picks, the artifacts it trusts, and the absolute paths it quietly rewrites all come from decisions encoded in the Ruby files under Library/Homebrew in the Homebrew/brew repository. That core is compact enough that a working developer can read all of it in an afternoon, which is rare for software with this much surface area, and it makes brew one of the better codebases to study if you maintain any installer, registry client, or dependency tool of your own.

The pain brew solves is not merely “install things”. It is three specific problems you hit the first time you manage more than one Mac or Linux box. First, dependency resolution: something must always exist before something else, and the ordering has to survive optional dependencies, recommended ones, and cycles. Second, formula versioning: postgres@14 and postgres@16 must coexist while brew upgrade still does the right thing for unversioned names. Third, install reproducibility: build from source on two machines and you get two compiler personalities; brew’s default is to pour a prebuilt, attested bottle and only fall back to compiling when no bottle matches your platform.

Those three problems are handled by three mostly-separate subsystems: a loader chain that turns a name into a Ruby class, a recursive dependency expander with an explicit cycle guard, and a bottle-first installer that treats compilation as the exception. The rest of this post walks the subsystems in the order your package actually travels through them.

Overview: from the install command through formula resolution, dependency expansion, download strategies, and the pour into the Cellar.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • InstallCmd, L13 parses the brew install invocation, auto-installs the tap a named formula belongs to, then hands off to the installer.
  • Formulary.factory, L788 is the single resolution entry point: a name, alias, path, or URI all funnel through one cached dispatch.
  • FromAPILoader, L706 short-circuits core-tap names into JSON-loaded classes, skipping the tap checkout entirely.
  • Formula, L89 is the DSL base class; every formula file in homebrew-core is a Ruby class inheriting from it.
  • Dependency.expand, L223 walks the dependency graph recursively, applying prune and skip filters and merging repeats.
  • DownloadStrategyDetector.detect, L12 maps a URL or a symbol onto exactly one strategy class.
  • CurlDownloadStrategy, L9 handles plain HTTPS downloads, resolving redirects and resuming partial files.
  • CurlGitHubPackagesDownloadStrategy, L7 fetches bottles as OCI artifacts from ghcr.io.
  • Keg#link, L526 finally symlinks the installed keg into HOMEBREW_PREFIX with per-directory rules.

Detail: the loader hierarchy, the SoftwareSpec model, the expand-and-merge dependency algorithm with its cycle guard, the strategy classes, and the pour/link/receipt storage layer.

Formulas are Ruby classes, not YAML

The first thing to internalize is that a formula is code, not data. formula.rb runs 5,532 lines on the branch this tour reads, and it defines the DSL every formula author touches. The convenience methods are thin delegates: url, L4500 forwards to the active stable spec, as do version, L4514 and bottle, L4574, while depends_on, L4821 and conflicts_with, L4954 register edges in metadata arrays. The spec objects themselves are SoftwareSpec, L17 instances holding the URL, checksums, and an optional bottle block, L177; a formula carries two of them, stable and head, exposed at L180 and L191.

The build hook is famously empty: def install; end, L3587 is a no-op that subclasses override with system "make", "install" style steps. Everything around it — checksum verification, unpacking, chdir into buildpath — is provided by the framework, which is why the average formula stays under fifty lines. Versioning rides the same class: versioned_formula?, L699 is literally name.include?("@"), and the whole node@20/node@22 pattern falls out of that one predicate. If you have read our Ruby source tour, the code style will feel familiar: Sorbet sig blocks, # typed: strict headers, and OS-specific behavior split into extend/os/mac and extend/os/linux override files rather than scattered conditionals.

From git taps to a JSON API

Resolution has two generations living side by side. The old one assumes taps are git checkouts under Library/Taps, parsed by FromTapLoader, L502 — still the path for third-party taps. The new one, used by default for homebrew/core, is a JSON API: API.fetch_json_api_file, L50 downloads formula.json into a local cache, API::Formula.fetch_api!, L128 triggers the refresh, and download_and_cache_data!, L141 rebuilds alias and rename indexes in a single pass over that file. all_formulae, L162 lazily initializes the whole thing on first lookup.

The loader hierarchy in formulary.rb (1,117 lines) is where the dispatch lives: a base FormulaLoader, L311 with specialized subclasses — FromBottleLoader, L377, FromPathLoader, L447, FromTapLoader, L502, FromKegLoader, L618, FromURILoader, L655, FromCacheLoader, L669, and FromAPILoader, L706 — each answering try_new queries. There are also two composite loaders worth knowing: FromNameLoader, L573, which subclasses the tap loader for plain names, and FormulaJSONContentsLoader, L759, which builds a formula class directly from JSON contents with no file involved at all. The API path is opt-out via no_install_from_api?, L712, which reads the HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_FROM_API environment switch. Formulary.factory, L788 caps it off with a factory cache keyed "name:#{ref}-#{spec}-#{alias_path}" so repeated lookups during one run are nearly free.

Dependency resolution: recursion with a guard rail

Dependency, L10 is a small edge object — a name, tags, options, and hidden or recommended state — and to_formula, L58 resolves it into a real formula when needed. The algorithm is Dependency.expand, L223, a class method defined under class << self: it pushes the dependent’s name onto an @expand_stack (L227), iterates the declared deps, and asks a filter block for one of three verdicts — prune, skip, or keep-but-stop-recursing — before recursing into each dependency’s own formula (L254). The stack is the cycle guard: a dependency loop is detected by name membership and simply skipped rather than crashing the install. Results are deduplicated by merge_repeats, L263, and the stack pops in an ensure block so exceptions cannot corrupt it.

The installer side consumes this: compute_dependencies, L703 turns the expanded set into an ordered plan, verify_deps_exist, L403 fails fast on unknown names, and install_dependency, L962 constructs one FormulaInstaller per dependency — the recursion you see in the terminal is literally a nested installer. When you force a source build and any dependency lacks a bottle, UnbottledError, L580 stops the run before half the tree is compiled.

Download strategies: one URL, many classes

download_strategy.rb is only 53 lines long, and almost all of it is a require list (L24 through L42) wiring the 19 strategy files that live in Library/Homebrew/download_strategy/. The brain is DownloadStrategyDetector.detect, L12: detect_from_url (L32) pattern-matches the URL — git hosts get GitDownloadStrategy, L9 with its shallow clone_repo, L279; ghcr.io hosts get the GitHub Packages subclass; everything else lands on CurlDownloadStrategy, L9, whose fetch, L40 resolves redirects and resumes partial downloads. VCS strategies share a common ancestor in VCSDownloadStrategy, L9.

A formula can also force a strategy with the :using symbol, but the choice is policed: HOMEBREW_CONTROLLED_STRATEGIES, L44 whitelists exactly the seven curl-family strategies a formula may select. Resources declared inside a formula (Resource, L14, fetched at L221) ride the same detector, which is how one formula pulls several unrelated tarballs and patches through one consistent integrity check.

From brew install to a linked keg: build facts from the tree

The install sequence ties everything together, and the code reads like a checklist. FormulaInstaller#install, L559 locks the formula (L560), runs build-from-source checks when no bottle can be poured (L563), checks conflicts (L578), computes and installs dependencies (L583, L591). Whether to pour is decided by pour_bottle?, L263; the Formula-side default is pour_bottle? = true (L1661) — pour unless a formula opts out.

The pour itself (pour, L1729) stages the Bottle, L8 tarball into the Cellar (Bottle#stage, L253), reloads the tab, stamps poured_from_bottle = true (L1762), persists it with tab.write, L1774, and then calls replace_placeholders_with_locations, L1787 to rewrite the absolute paths baked in at build time. The receipt is AbstractTab, L11 with FILENAME = "INSTALL_RECEIPT.json" (L18); the concrete Tab, L4 subclass adds formula-specific fields, and Tab.create, L94 plus from_file, L114 bracket its lifecycle. Downloads are queued up-front by enqueue_fetch, L1626 with a Sigstore attestation check attached (verify_bottle_attestation?, L1684) — bottles are verified before anything is unpacked. When pouring is not possible, the fallback path is equally explicit: build, L630 runs the formula’s install hook, then Tab.clear_cache and a cleanup pass wipe anything the build left behind. Linking is Keg#link, L526 in the 996-line keg.rb: an opt link pass (L531) followed by link_dir rules for etc, bin, sbin, include and share (L535 onward), each directory getting its own mkpath/skip policy — which is exactly why some config files land in /etc while binaries end up in bin. For scale: cmd/ holds 76 user-facing command files, dev-cmd/ another 70, and the 2,052-line installer swaps mac/linux behavior through extend/os overrides rather than inline if statements.

Honest Limits

Line numbers here come from main at commit b43c73f8 on 2026-11-18; brew lands hundreds of commits a month, so treat the anchors as a snapshot, not a stable API. Coverage is partial by design: casks have their own installer under Library/Homebrew/cask/, and services, livecheck, and the RuboCop suite are entirely out of scope. The pour flow described assumes standard ghcr.io bottles — mirror setups go through different relocation logic and are flagged with a warning in the code. Finally, FormulaInstaller is an internal class with no stability promise; if you script against it, pin the commit. One connection worth noting: because versioned formulae are just ordinary classes with an @ in the name, parallel Node.js installs on one machine fall out of the same machinery for free — no lockfile, no plugin, just naming.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Homebrew's Ruby core: formula classes, loader chains, download strategies, dependency expansion and the bottle pour into the Cellar.

entry.title: How Cargo Works: Dependency Resolution, Registry Cache, and Cargo.lock Internals

link.title: How Cargo Works: Dependency Resolution, Registry Cache, and Cargo.lock Internals

entry.content:
Every developer eventually meets the same nightmare in a different language: two packages want incompatible versions of the same dependency, the installer prints a wall of conflict errors, and you spend your afternoon hand-pinning versions until the build passes again. In the Rust ecosystem this problem is handled by cargo, and the way it handles it is worth reading in the source. The resolver documentation in src/resolver/mod.rs opens with a refreshingly honest admission: actually solving a dependency constraint graph is an NP-hard problem, and what cargo implements is “a nice heuristic to make sure we get roughly the best answer most of the time.” That single comment frames the entire design philosophy of the tool.

The second pain cargo attacks is the “works on my machine” problem. If you have ever committed a package-lock.json, uv.lock, or poetry.lock file, you have used cargo’s idea: record the exact set of versions (and their checksums) that were resolved once, so every teammate and every CI runner builds from the same inputs. Cargo.lock is not an afterthought in the codebase; it has its own versioned serialization format, a dedicated encode/decode module, and logic that refuses to rewrite the file when nothing changed. Reading how it is produced explains a lot about why Rust builds are so reproducible.

The third pain is speed and disk usage. crates.io hosts hundreds of thousands of crates, and downloading the full metadata index for all of them just to install one crate would be absurd. Cargo therefore layers several caches between your build and the network: an in-memory summary cache, an on-disk key-value cache of index entries, a .package-cache file lock guarding concurrent access, and a SQLite database that tracks what is stored so old artifacts can be garbage-collected. This post walks the real code of rust-lang/cargo at commit level, with two architecture diagrams built from the actual tree.

Overview of cargo: the command layer drives the resolver, which queries package sources and records the result in Cargo.lock, while cache locks keep concurrent cargo processes from trampling each other.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • resolve, L125 is the entry point of dependency resolution: a depth-first search that activates the highest version first and backtracks through a backtrack_stack when a choice dead-ends.
  • VersionPreferences, L33 decides which summaries are preferred over others, including a PublishAgePolicy that can demote crates published too recently to have proven themselves.
  • RegistryQueryer, L204 sits between the resolver and the package sources, caching which Dependency requests were already answered for a given activation.
  • Source, L32 is the trait every package source implements — registry, git, path, or directory — and SourceMap pools them during a build.
  • RegistrySource, L246 is the crates.io implementation; the same file pins the default index as sparse+https://index.crates.io/.
  • HttpRegistry, L66 fetches config.json and index files over HTTP, keeping the registry configuration in a short-lived in-memory cache.
  • CacheManager, L225 persists parsed index summaries to disk with simple get/put/invalidate operations keyed by index version.
  • CacheLocker, L474 serializes cache access across concurrent cargo processes using a lock file literally named .package-cache.
  • write_pkg_lockfile, L46 writes Cargo.lock but deliberately skips the write when the serialized output is byte-identical to what is already on disk.

Detail view: each command entry point funnels through workspace resolution; the resolver's context, dep cache, and error types cooperate; registry, git, path, and directory sources plug into one Source trait; file locks and SQLite bookkeeping protect the shared cache.

The Resolver: NP-Hard by Nature, Pragmatic by Design

The heart of src/resolver/mod.rs is a DFS over “DepsFrames.” For each package it activates, the resolver collects the package’s dependencies into a frame, tries the highest compatible version first (because semver-compatible ranges mean the newest version is most likely to satisfy everyone), and records a backtrack frame so it can return to a previous choice if a conflict appears. Conflicts are recorded in a ConflictMap: the resolver knows that activating crate X at version A conflicts with crate Y at version B, and uses that knowledge to avoid retrying doomed combinations.

Two design details deserve attention. First, the resolver runs twice per build in the current code: once with all features enabled (this run produces what is saved to Cargo.lock) and once with only the user-selected features — the module documentation flags the second run as legacy behavior that ideally goes away as the newer feature resolver from 2020 takes over. Second, version preference is not purely “highest wins”: VersionPreferences sorts summaries with configurable ordering, and the PublishAgePolicy machinery shows cargo experimenting with demoting brand-new releases, a direct response to supply-chain incidents across package ecosystems.

When resolution fails, the errors are as engineered as the success path. ResolveError carries the full package_path — the chain of packages that led to the conflict — because a bare “no matching version” message would be useless for a deep transitive conflict. Backtracking itself is bounded by heuristics like a “critical age” shortcircuit that stops the search from endlessly thrashing on huge graphs.

Inside the Registry Cache

The crates.io integration is split across src/sources/registry/. The RegistrySource in mod.rs is the orchestrator: it picks an index backend, queries it for summaries, and delegates downloads. http_remote.rs implements the sparse protocol used today: instead of cloning the whole index repository, cargo requests only the per-crate metadata files it needs, caching config.json and each response. The legacy GitRegistry in git_remote.rs still exists for indexes served from a cloned git repository, and local.rs provides a LocalRegistry that reads an on-disk index directory — useful for air-gapped environments and tests.

Metadata caching lives in index/cache.rs. SummariesCache is the in-memory parse of a cache blob, and CacheManager is the disk side: one file per key under a cache root, written with put, read with get, dropped with invalidate. The cache key includes an index version so stale summaries are naturally abandoned after format changes. Downloads of the actual .crate archives flow through download.rs, which tracks whether a crate is already downloaded, and every one of these operations runs under the .package-cache lock from util/cache_lock.rs so that a cargo build in one terminal cannot corrupt state while cargo fetch runs in another.

Going one level deeper, cargo has been moving cache bookkeeping into SQLite. The GlobalCacheTracker in src/workspace/global_cache_tracker.rs opens a database at $CARGO_HOME/.global-cache (the GLOBAL_CACHE_FILENAME constant, with db_path resolving the location) and maintains tables like RegistryIndex, RegistryCrate, RegistrySrc, GitDb, and GitCheckout. The comment at the top of that file explains the motivation: multiple cargo processes share the same cache, and a relational database with explicit locking semantics is more robust than hand-managed files. The migration helpers in src/util/sqlite.rs keep that schema upgradable without nuking users’ caches.

From Git Clones to Sparse HTTP, and Cargo.lock V1 to V4

Two migrations define the modern cargo experience, and both are visible as real code paths rather than folklore. The index migration: the constant CRATES_IO_HTTP_INDEX in src/sources/registry/mod.rs is set to sparse+https://index.crates.io/, and the code selects HTTP operations when the source id is sparse, falling back to GitRegistry only for old-style indexes. The lockfile migration: src/resolver/encode.rs decodes all four generations of the format. In V1, per-package checksums were stored in a separate [metadata] section of Cargo.lock; V2 folded checksums into the package blocks and moved dependency edges to a cleaner encoding; V3 and V4 followed, with the decoder mapping Some(4) to ResolveVersion::V4. The encoder also bumps the version when a lockfile needs features that older encodings cannot express — for example, V1 lockfiles are upgraded when checksums cannot be represented in the [metadata] section.

The engineering discipline around Cargo.lock is the third fact worth stealing: write_pkg_lockfile in src/ops/lockfile.rs serializes the resolve, compares it with the file already on disk, and writes nothing when they match. That is why checking out a repo and running an unrelated cargo command does not pollute your diffs with lockfile churn. When cargo update does change pins, print_lockfile_changes in src/ops/cargo_update.rs renders a colored before/after diff of the exact version changes. Related trivia: all fingerprint and cache-key hashing rides on a StableHasher (a stable 128-bit SipHash re-exported in src/util/hasher.rs), so hashes must not change when Rust’s std HashMap seed changes.

What Happens After Resolve

Once a Resolve exists, cargo’s command layer takes over. resolve_ws in src/ops/resolve.rs bridges the workspace and the resolver: it loads the previous lockfile if present, resolves with it as a preference, and produces the PackageSet of downloads. cargo_fetch.rs then walks the resolve and downloads every missing package. For build commands, ops/cargo_compile/mod.rs provides compile and create_bcx, which build the build context; the actual scheduling happens in the compiler module’s JobQueue, whose execute method runs the unit graph through a parallel job queue with fingerprint checks deciding what is stale. Publish closes the loop: publish in ops/registry/cargo_publish.rs packages the crate, verifies it, and uploads it through the same registry machinery used for downloads. If you want to see how a modern tool reimplements these ideas for Python, the uv source tour on this blog is the natural companion read.

Honest Limits

This walkthrough covers the resolution, registry, cache, and lockfile layers that make cargo distinctive; it does not cover the build compiler internals in depth. The src/compiler/ tree — unit graphs, fingerprint invalidation, build scripts, the timings reporter — is a substantial codebase of its own and was only touched at the entry points here. The diagrams also intentionally stop at module boundaries: they show what talks to what, not every helper function inside each file.

Two caveats about the code itself. First, the resolver documentation explicitly calls the algorithm a heuristic; pathological dependency graphs can still produce long resolution times or surprising version picks, which is why Cargo.lock exists in the first place. Second, cache internals are actively evolving — the SQLite-based global cache tracker and garbage collection are newer additions and their formats may still change between releases, so do not build tools that parse $CARGO_HOME internals. Finally, line numbers cited here refer to the master branch as of this writing; cargo moves fast, and functions may shift after the next release. For the git-based dependency machinery, our git internals tour covers the underlying version control that cargo drives through libgit2 and gitoxide.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of rust-lang/cargo: the backtracking resolver, the sparse HTTP registry cache, .package-cache locks, and Cargo.lock versions V1 to V4.

entry.title: How mamba Makes conda Installs Fast: Inside the libsolv Resolver and C++ Core

link.title: How mamba Makes conda Installs Fast: Inside the libsolv Resolver and C++ Core

entry.content:
Every data scientist knows the pain: you type conda install pytorch, the solver grinds for five minutes, and you stare at “Solving environment: - \ … failed” while a build server idles. The old conda front end resolved dependencies in Python, re-reading repodata and rebuilding state on every invocation. For a 300-package ML stack — numpy, pytorch, cuda, cudnn, their transitive dependency trees — that cost compounds with every environment you clone or CI job you run. This post is a source tour of the mamba package manager — the C++ reimplementation that made conda installs fast. (To be clear for readers who landed here from ML papers: this is not the state-space Mamba model; it is the package manager behind mamba and micromamba commands.)

The pain is worse than slow installs. ML stacks must be reproducible: the same training run on your laptop, the CI runner, and the cluster needs byte-identical dependency sets. conda addressed that with lockfiles, and mamba implements the machinery in C++ — read_environment_lockfile at env_lockfile.cpp, L48 parses a pinned lockfile and install_lockfile_specs at install.cpp, L837 replays it into an environment without re-solving, which is exactly what a reproducible build needs.

The speed, meanwhile, is not one trick. It is four deliberate engineering decisions visible directly in the repository: a SAT solver written for package management (libsolv) driven from C++ instead of Python; repodata caches that survive process restarts, including a newer “sharded” format that downloads only the metadata slices it needs; parallel downloads through libcurl’s multi interface; and a transaction layer that links files into your prefix with hardlinks instead of re-copying tarballs. We verified every claim below against the actual tree on the main branch at commit d52ba4737acd, so the line numbers are real.

The repository layout tells the story before you read a line of code. micromamba/ holds the standalone C++ executable; libmamba/ is the C++ core library — src/api for command implementations, src/solver for the resolver, src/core for transactions, caches and channels, src/download for the network layer; and libmambapy/ exposes the core to Python via pybind11. One detail worth noting: the classic Python mamba package is gone from main — the CLI itself is C++ now, and the Python layer is a thin binding, not the engine.

Overview of mamba's install flow: the micromamba CLI reaches the API layer, which resolves channels, loads repodata into a libsolv database, solves, then executes the resulting transaction through the package cache and linking engine.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L179 is the executable entry point; it builds a CLI11 command tree and delegates to set_umamba_command in umamba.cpp, L130, which registers the create and install subcommands.
  • install_specs, L713 is the heart of the install flow: it loads configuration, builds a solver Database, and later constructs the MTransaction at install.cpp, L1302.
  • ChannelContext::make_channel, L251 turns a channel name or URL into concrete Channel objects with mirrors, so downloads can later fall back across them.
  • SubdirIndexLoader::maybe_set_shards_from_cache, L517 checks whether a cached shard index is fresh enough to skip the full repodata download entirely.
  • Database::add_repo_from_repodata_json, L152 feeds channel metadata into the libsolv pool; a sibling method at database.cpp, L221 reloads it from a native .solv serialization instead.
  • request_to_decision_queue, L1742 converts install/update/remove jobs into the raw libsolv job queue.
  • Solver::solve, L95 sets libsolv flags (downgrade, uninstall, strict repo priority at solver.cpp, L23) and runs solver->solve(pool, jobs) at solver.cpp, L71, then converts the libsolv transaction into a Solution at solver.cpp, L80.
  • MTransaction::execute, L532 runs the plan: fetch, extract, unlink removed packages at transaction.cpp, L787, link new ones at transaction.cpp, L831.
  • CURLMultiHandle, L531 caps concurrent transfers with CURLMOPT_MAX_TOTAL_CONNECTIONS at curl.cpp, L543, so hundreds of package downloads proceed in parallel.

The detail view adds the specs parsers, sharded repodata machinery, mirror handling, unsolvable-conflict rendering, and the pybind11 layer that keeps libmambapy a wrapper rather than a reimplementation.

Where the Time Goes: libsolv, Not Python

The single biggest win is architectural. libsolv is a satisfiability solver that originated in openSUSE’s package management; it operates on a pool of “solvables” and solves joint constraints natively in C. mamba embeds it through thin wrappers in libmamba/ext/solv-cpp/ — ObjSolver, ObjPool, ObjTransaction — instead of talking to the C API directly. The wrapper header for the solver declares class ObjSolver with a single solve(const ObjPool& pool, const ObjQueue& jobs) -> bool, and solver.cpp, L77 derives an ordered ObjTransaction straight from the solver result.

What makes it feel fast is also what happens before the solve. The installed prefix is loaded into the same database as a repo — see load_installed_packages_in_database at package_database_loader.cpp, L154 — so the solver reasons about what is already there rather than diffing Python dictionaries afterwards. And when a solve fails, mamba does not dump raw libsolv noise: ProblemsGraph in problems_graph.cpp, L53 simplifies conflicts, and problems_graph.cpp, L586 compresses them into the readable “nothing provides X needed by Y” reports you see in the terminal. Debugging a failed environment is as much part of the experience as installing one.

Repodata Caching: From Full JSON to Shards

conda-forge repodata is enormous — hundreds of megabytes of JSON per platform when uncompressed. mamba attacks this at two levels. The classic level: subdir_index.cpp maintains per-channel caches, and a small state file (.state.json, written next to the cache, see subdir_index.cpp, L178) records whether the cached JSON or libsolv .solv file is still valid — valid_libsolv_cache_path at subdir_index.cpp, L582 hands that pre-serialized pool straight to the solver. This is why a second mamba install in the same session starts solving in milliseconds.

The newer level is sharded repodata. Instead of one giant JSON, the channel publishes an index plus many small shards keyed by package name, and mamba fetches only what the current request can touch. subdir_index.cpp, L517 loads the shard index from cache when it is fresh enough, ShardIndexLoader::fetch_and_parse_shard_index at shard_index_loader.cpp, L527 fetches it when not, and shard_traversal.cpp, L221 walks the shard graph fetching only the slices that match your specs. Installing one package no longer means downloading the universe.

Fetch, Validate, Link: The Transaction Engine

A solved Solution is just a list of package identities; the interesting engineering is in applying it. MTransaction::execute takes a LockFile on the prefix’s conda-meta directory at transaction.cpp, L573, so two concurrent installs cannot corrupt one environment. It fetches everything first — fetch_extract_packages at transaction.cpp, L1101 — before mutating anything.

Downloads themselves go through PackageFetcher (package_fetcher.cpp, L141), which first queries MultiPackageCache — multiple cache directories, the first writable one chosen by package_cache.cpp, L556 — for existing tarballs or extracted copies (get_tarball_path at package_cache.cpp, L606). Only cache misses hit the network, where downloader.cpp, L1314 runs all requests through the libcurl multi interface with mirror fallback via mirror_map::get_mirrors at mirror_map.cpp, L31. Every download is verified — size at package_fetcher.cpp, L443, checksum at package_fetcher.cpp, L457 — before it counts as fetched. The execute path also honors the operational modes you expect in CI: dry runs that print the plan without touching the prefix (transaction.cpp, L556) and a download-only mode that stops after fetch and extraction (transaction.cpp, L592).

The linking phase is where mamba quietly outperforms naive unpacking. LinkPackage::execute at link.cpp, L1252 walks each package’s file list; link_path at link.cpp, L933 records "hardlink" as the common path_type (link.cpp, L1329), meaning the file appears in your prefix as a hardlink into the shared cache — zero data copying in the common case. noarch Python packages get entry-point scripts generated at link.cpp, L348, and compile_pyc_files at link.cpp, L1225 precompiles bytecode so first import is fast. If anything fails mid-transaction, LinkPackage::undo at link.cpp, L1562 supports rolling the prefix back — the history module that powers mamba list --revisions parses the same conda-meta records at history.cpp, L40.

From Python Glue to a C++ Core

The migration story is visible in build artifacts. Today libmambapy/bindings/bindings.cpp starts with PYBIND11_MODULE(bindings, m) at bindings.cpp, L9 and registers submodules — utils, specs, solver, libsolv, logging — at bindings.cpp, L11. The Python layer binds the C++ Database class directly at solver_libsolv.cpp, L134; there is no duplicated solver logic to keep in sync. The same is true of configuration: .condarc/.mambarc files are recognized by the C++ configuration loader at configuration.cpp, L1097, and spec strings like numpy==1.26 are parsed by MatchSpec::parse at match_spec.cpp, L539 — one parser, shared by CLI, Python API, and solver jobs.

This “from Python glue to C++ core” shift is the same pattern that made other package managers fast. uv tipped the Python wheel ecosystem the same way — replace the interpreter-loop front end with a compiled engine, keep the format compatible. In conda’s ecosystem the analogous rewrite lives in pixi, which keeps the channel-and-repodata model while rebuilding the tooling in Rust; mamba proves the C++ route first. And because mamba manipulates the CPython installation itself — relinking noarch packages when the interpreter changes is handled explicitly by solution_needs_python_relink at solver.cpp, L82, with add_noarch_relink_to_solution following at solver.cpp, L84 — knowing how CPython locates its own files and bytecode makes the pyc and entry-point handling much less mysterious.

Honest Limits

  • Speed depends on channel state. The first-ever solve on a machine still downloads full (or sharded) repodata; the caching described above only pays off after the first run, and .state.json invalidates when the remote moves.
  • libsolv is a shared dependency. mamba inherits libsolv’s behaviors, including sensitivity to job ordering — the code even documents it at solver.cpp, L31 with a determinism workaround.
  • The Python mamba package is gone on main. Scripts importing mamba should migrate to libmambapy; older releases keep the legacy layout.
  • Hardlinks require the cache and the prefix to share a filesystem. Cross-drive setups fall back to copies, and that path is slower by nature.
  • Sharded repodata needs server support. On channels that only publish classic repodata, the shard traversal is simply unused.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of mamba, the fast conda package manager: how its libsolv resolver, parallel downloads, and hardlink-heavy transaction make installs quick.

entry.title: Nix Internals: How the /nix/store, Derivations, and the Daemon Actually Work

link.title: Nix Internals: How the /nix/store, Derivations, and the Daemon Actually Work

entry.content:
Every developer has lost an afternoon to “works on my machine”. You upgrade OpenSSL, half your toolchain silently links against the old one, and the bug reproduces on exactly one laptop. Traditional package managers install files into shared directories like /usr/lib, so every upgrade mutates the one environment you have. Nix refuses that premise entirely: nothing is ever mutated. Every package lands in a path like /nix/store/5x7k9...-openssl-3.4.1, where the hash prefix encodes the exact build inputs that produced it. Two builds with different inputs cannot collide, and an upgrade cannot corrupt what already exists, because nothing is ever overwritten.

The second promise you hear about is rollbacks. Nix builds you a numbered generation of your environment, and switching back to yesterday is a symlink flip, not a reinstall. That sounds like marketing until you read the code and find that rollback really is one function, switchGeneration, flipping one symlink in one directory. The immutability of the store is what makes it safe: old generations keep working because their paths still exist, byte-identical, on disk. And when disk fills up, garbage collection walks the reference graph from live roots and deletes exactly the paths nothing points at anymore — no registry, no uninstaller, just reachability.

This post is a source-level tour of NixOS/nix at commit bada5b254b3a on master — the C++ implementation, not the Nix language itself. The layout is clean once you know the map: src/libexpr is the evaluator, src/libstore is the store plus daemon plus build engine, and src/nix holds the modern CLI. The codebase is genuinely pleasant to read — the daemon’s entire protocol is one switch statement, and the sandbox is a few hundred lines of namespace plumbing you can follow with a hot drink. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual tree, and the two diagrams were generated from that same source. Let’s start wide.

The whole system in one picture: a CLI layer that evaluates Nix expressions, an abstract store API with LocalStore as the on-disk implementation, a goal-based build engine, and a versioned daemon protocol in front of it all.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L603 parses argv and dispatches into the command table built by RegisterCommand::getCommandsFor at L193; every subcommand self-registers from its own translation unit.
  • CmdBuild, L109 is nix build. Its run at L152 calls Installable::build with a Realise::Outputs mode — “give me the actual store outputs, not just the plan”.
  • EvalState, L241 is the evaluator core; its constructor calls createBaseEnv at L383, which populates builtins before any file is parsed.
  • prim_derivationStrict, L1439 is the primitive that turns an attribute set into a real derivation and registers it in the store; the registration site is static RegisterPrimOp primop_derivationStrict at L1945.
  • derivation builtin, L36 — surprisingly, derivation itself is a .nix file that just wraps derivationStrict, evaluated once at evaluator startup.
  • Store::queryPathInfo, L585 is the abstract store interface asking “is this path valid, and what does it reference?” — subclasses answer it for disk, HTTP caches, or SSH remotes.
  • LocalStore, L126 owns the actual /nix/store directory and its SQLite metadata database.
  • Worker::run, L283 is the build scheduler: a coroutine loop over Goal objects that drives derivations and substitutions to completion.
  • performOp, L317 is the daemon’s giant switch over protocol operations — the bridge between a client process and all of the above.

The detail view adds the machinery: protocol op codes, SQLite registration, the goal engine, substituter fetches, and the platform-specific sandbox builders under src/libstore/linux/build and src/libstore/unix/build.

The Store Path Is Its Own Specification

The hash in /nix/store/... is not a hash of the file contents — it is a hash of a small text string that specifies how the path was produced. StoreDirConfig::makeStorePath, L85 builds the string type + ":" + hash + ":" + storeDir + ":" + name (the comment in the code even spells out source:sha256:1abc...:/nix/store:foo.tar.gz), runs SHA-256 over it, and then compressHash(..., 20) at L89 folds the 32-byte digest down to 20 bytes. References matter: makeType, L106 appends every referenced store path into the type string, so depending on a different build of a library changes your hash. The path name literally encodes its dependency graph.

The rendering is quirky on purpose. StorePath’s constructor, L49 validates the basename and rejects any hash character from the set e, o, u, t at L55 — a trimmed base-32 alphabet. path.hh, L41 fixes HashLen = 32 (32 characters × 5 bits = 160 bits), and the comment at L46 gives the engineering reason: HashLen + MaxNameLen + 1 (dash) + len("/nix/store/") = 255, exactly the classic filename limit. Even the metadata is content-addressed: ValidPathInfo records a narHash at L75 plus the sorted references at L80.

Underneath, the store’s database is plain SQLite: LocalStore::openDB, L516 opens db.sqlite and, at L554, selects WAL journaling for concurrency. Registration is transactional — registerValidPaths, L986 commits a batch of ValidPathInfo rows in one go, which is why a crashed build never leaves the store’s metadata half-written.

What deletes things is just as principled. LocalStore::collectGarbage, L372 first asks what is alive: findRootsNoTemp, L308 scans two directories — the GC roots directory under the state dir and profiles at L311-L312 — and follows every symlink it finds. From those roots, the collector transitsively walks the references edges each ValidPathInfo carries and deletes everything unreachable. Nothing can be deleted out from under a running environment because anything in use has a root pointing at it; that is the entire guarantee, and it fits in one sentence precisely because the data model made it expressible.

The Evaluator: derivation Is Just a .nix File

The Nix language’s most important builtin is not C++ at all. At startup the evaluator registers derivation as a constant — primops.cc, L5609 allocates the value and L5625 evaluates it from derivationInternal, a virtual file injected at eval.cc, L301. The real content is derivation.nix, whose own comment says it is “a wrapper around the derivationStrict primop”. At L36 it calls strict = derivationStrict drvAttrs, then builds a lazy attribute set exposing outPath and drvPath for each output.

Why wrap it? derivationStrict does the heavy lifting — force the strings, compute the fixed-output or text content address, register the .drv — while the wrapper keeps the result lazy: outPath expands to a placeholder that the build engine later realises. Only forcing an outPath (by nix build, or by import, readFile, readDir — the “import from derivation” cases listed right in the file’s doc comment) forces a build. This is the trick that makes Nix expressions feel declarative while remaining cheap: evaluating ten thousand packages does not build anything until something actually consumes an output path. EvalState::evalFile, L1162 and parseExprFromFile at L3242 handle the parse tree side; the biggest single file in the evaluator is primops.cc at roughly 212 KB, where all the builtins live as static RegisterPrimOp objects — including the derived-path plumbing that converts lazy attribute strings into concrete DerivedPath requests.

Builds: Goals, Sandboxes, and Two Stores

One subtlety most users never see: the evaluator uses a separate store just for .drv files. Worker’s constructor, L20 takes Store & store, Store & evalStore as two distinct references, so evaluation churn (thousands of .drv files) never pollutes your runtime closure.

The build engine is a goal graph. LocalBuilder::buildPaths, L11 is the bridge from the store API into Worker::buildPaths, L45, which queues top-level goals; Worker::run, L283 then loops forever (L289) waking goals as dependencies finish. Worker::makeGoal, L130 decides per-request whether you get a DerivationGoal (build it) or a PathSubstitutionGoal (someone else built it — fetch it). DerivationGoal::haveDerivation, L55 checks validity first and only builds what’s actually missing.

The sandbox is the part that surprises people: Nix builds use the same kernel primitives as container runtimes like containerd. On Linux, ChrootLinuxDerivationBuilder::prepareSandbox, L513 assembles the chroot, and startChild at L527 spawns the child with options.cloneFlags = CLONE_NEWPID | CLONE_NEWNS | CLONE_NEWIPC | CLONE_NEWUTS at L596, conditionally CLONE_NEWNET and CLONE_NEWUSER at L598 and L600. New PID and mount namespaces, optionally no network — isolation by construction, not by convention. After the build, registerOutputs, L106 verifies outputs against the derivation’s declared constraints and registers them.

Substitution is the mirror image of building. When a path is missing but a binary cache has it, PathSubstitutionGoal::substitute, L38 queries each configured substituter — its callback at L88 calls sub->queryPathInfo — and tryToRun, L197 starts the actual NAR download. The binary cache model means most users never build most packages; the goal engine just picks the cheapest source that can satisfy a hash. The two goals share the same Worker loop and the same validity checks, so a substituted path and a locally built path are indistinguishable afterwards — both are just rows in the same SQLite database with the same narHash verification.

The Daemon: A Versioned Protocol, Not a REST API

nix daemon is CmdDaemon, L658; its accept loop, daemonLoop, L275, listens on a Unix socket created with mode 0666 at L381. Each connection is served by daemon::processConnection, L19, which carries a TrustedFlag — untrusted clients get a allowlisted world: daemon.cc, L297 quietly ignores their settings with “restricted setting and you are not a trusted user”.

The wire format is defined by the WorkerProto::Op enum at worker-protocol.hh, L235, and its discipline is worth copying. Operations are numbered forever: IsValidPath = 1 at L236, BuildPaths = 9 at L243, BuildPathsWithResults = 46 at L278. Removed ops stay as commented-out tombstones (// HasSubstitutes = 3, // removed) so numbers are never reused. The handshake, WorkerProto::ClientHandshakeInfo at L287, exchanges the daemon’s version string and a three-state trust value — “yes”, “no”, or unknown — because the server cannot always prove who is on the other end of the socket. The version handshake is two macros: PROTOCOL_VERSION (1 << 8 | 39) — i.e. 2.39 — at L18 and a floor of 2.18 at L19. Every op lands in performOp’s switch, L317: AddToStore at L450, BuildPaths at L592, CollectGarbage at L794. One function, fifty operations, zero web frameworks.

From SHA-256 to a Store Path: Build Facts

A few concrete engineering facts pulled straight from the tree:

  • The digest fold is XOR-based: compressHash in src/libutil/hash.cc XORs each byte of the 32-byte SHA-256 into hash[i % 20] — five wraps, twenty bytes, no padding scheme.
  • 20 bytes render as exactly 32 characters of Nix’s custom base-32 (5 bits per char), and the alphabet drops e/o/u/t — 32 chars of high-entropy gibberish that also can’t spell words.
  • The 255-byte basename budget is a designed constraint, not luck — see the path.hh comment above.
  • Fixed-output builds (downloads pinned by hash) have their own name math: makeFixedOutputPath at store-dir-config.cc, L117, with Git-style ingestion restricted to SHA-1/SHA-256 at L119 — one of several places git semantics reach into the store model.
  • Storage dedup is a hardlink farm: optimisePath_, L105 hashes file contents by inode and calls create_hard_link into the .links directory at L192 — identical copies of a library across 40 packages cost one copy on disk.
  • Rollback really is small: createGeneration at profiles.cc, L61 writes a numbered generation symlink, and switchGeneration, L252 points the profile back at an older one.
  • The build system is Meson, with a top-level meson.build; as of this commit the master tree contains no Rust sources at all — the daemon protocol handling cited above is C++ end to end.

Honest Limits

  • This tour reflects one commit (bada5b254b3a) of a fast-moving master. Line numbers drift; the architecture usually doesn’t.
  • We focused on Linux. Darwin and FreeBSD have their own builders under src/libstore/darwin/build and src/libstore/freebsd/build, including chroot variants we didn’t inspect.
  • Coverage is deliberately partial: the fetcher subsystem (src/libfetchers), flakes (src/libflake), and the HTTP/S3 substituter internals (binary-cache-store.cc, s3-binary-cache-store.cc) each deserve their own post.
  • The coroutine-based goal engine (Goal::Co in goal.cc) and the eval-gc machinery are subtle enough that a diagram flattens them; treat the graphs as maps, not spec.
  • If you want the sandbox mechanics compared against real container runtimes, pair this with a look at runc; if you want the “why” of content addressing, the store-path section above plus the SQLite schema in local-store.cc is the fastest path.
entry.summary: A guided tour through Nix's C++ source: how /nix/store hashes path names, how derivations build in sandboxes, and what the daemon protocol really speaks.

entry.title: How Pacman Works: Inside libalpm’s Dependency Resolution and Local Database in C

link.title: How Pacman Works: Inside libalpm’s Dependency Resolution and Local Database in C

entry.content:
Run pacman -Syu on Arch Linux and a 25,000-line C program will decide, in a fraction of a second, the exact order in which hundreds of packages get replaced on your root filesystem — and it will refuse to run at all if the resolution says the result would tear the system apart. That decision lives in lib/libalpm, the Arch Linux Package Manager library that the pacman binary in src/pacman is really just a thin command-line skin over. The two halves ship together in the pacman repository, and the split is the whole design: everything dangerous — dependency math, database writes, downloads, hooks — happens inside libalpm behind a small C API, and the CLI only parses arguments and renders progress bars.

The first pain this architecture solves is dependency hell in its most concrete form: an upgrade where package A needs a newer library than package B provides, half-applied. pacman’s answer is transactional. Nothing is computed piecemeal while installing; instead the entire change set is resolved against the databases first, sorted into a safe order, checked for conflicts, and only then handed to an install or remove phase that either completes or rolls the system back to a consistent state.

The second pain is local database integrity. pacman has no SQL engine — the installed-package database under $localstatedir/lib/pacman/ is a directory tree of plain text files, one directory per package, which any script can read but which pacman must defend against format drift and corruption. The third pain is trusting a mirror: package databases and packages themselves are downloaded over plain HTTP mirrors by default, so signatures are checked with GPGME, and since the 6.x era the download itself can run as an unprivileged sandbox user with seccomp filtering its syscalls.

Overview: the CLI skin, the libalpm core, the dependency engine, and the two database backends with the downloader underneath.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L1178 dispatches the parsed operation — sync, query, remove, upgrade — after parseargs, L964 has translated getopt output into flags.
  • alpm_initialize, L37 binds a root directory and a database path into the single alpm_handle_t every later call goes through.
  • local_db_populate, L533 walks the on-disk local database and builds the in-memory package cache.
  • alpm_db_update, L139 is what -Sy actually calls: it refreshes one or more sync databases from their mirrors.
  • alpm_checkdeps, L300 compares the would-be world against the current one and returns every dependency that would go missing.
  • _alpm_sortbydeps, L213 topologically orders the targets so a library always lands before the programs that link it.
  • alpm_sync_sysupgrade, L200 computes the full upgrade set that -Su will propose.
  • alpm_trans_commit, L167 executes the prepared transaction — load, verify, run hooks, install or remove.
  • _alpm_hook_run, L528 fires the hooks from /usr/share/libalpm/hooks before and after that commit.

Detail: the CLI commands, the handle and transaction state machine, the dependency engine's internals, the operation layer, and the store plus network halves of libalpm.

The local database is a directory tree, not SQLite

The default database path is compiled in as DBPATH — $localstatedir/lib/pacman/ (meson.build, L73) — and the installed-package database is the backend registered under the treename "local" (be_local.c, L1215). There is no server and no query language. local_db_populate, L533 does a bare readdir over that directory, splits each entry name into package name and version with _alpm_splitname, and inserts the result into a hashed cache built by _alpm_pkghash_create, L61. Lazily, when a caller asks for more detail, local_db_read, L713 parses the desc and depends text files inside the package’s directory. Writes go the same way: after a successful install, _alpm_local_db_write, L972 regenerates those files from the in-memory package struct.

Format drift is guarded by a version file: local_db_validate, L444 looks for ALPM_DB_VERSION (written at L489) and fails loudly if an old database lacks it, which is what pacman-db-upgrade exists to migrate. For file-level integrity, each package directory can carry an mtree manifest; _cache_mtree_open, L251 opens it through libarchive, and the consumer is the -Qkk checker in check.c, L314, which compares recorded digests against what is actually on disk. The public surface for all of this is small: alpm_register_syncdb, L40 attaches named repositories, and alpm_db_search, L346 is the substring search behind pacman -Ss.

Dependency resolution: satisfiers, not a solver

There is no SAT solver anywhere in libalpm. A dependency string like glibc>=2.38 is parsed by alpm_dep_from_string, L458 into a name, an operator, and a version, and satisfaction is decided by dep_vercmp, L392, a hand-rolled comparison that understands pacman’s epoch-version-release scheme. Finding a provider is a scan, not a search: find_dep_satisfier, L86 walks one package list, and the general case resolvedep, L636 checks what is already installed first, then walks the sync databases in the order pacman.conf lists them — which is exactly why mirror-less users who reorder their repos see different choices.

alpm_checkdeps, L300 is the safety net: it simulates the removal set and reports every depmissing that would result, which is how pacman refuses pacman -R glibc. Ordering comes from dep_graph_init, L104, which builds a vertex graph over the targets, and _alpm_sortbydeps, L213, a depth-first topological sort whose cycle handling is deliberately forgiving — _alpm_warn_dep_cycle, L161 logs a warning and moves on rather than aborting, because provision loops are legal in Arch packaging. If you have read our uv source tour, the contrast is stark: uv must search a universe of published versions under tight latency budgets, while pacman resolves a single, already-materialized world and can afford plain list scans.

The transaction is a strict state machine

Every change goes through the same five calls: alpm_trans_init, L45 with flags like ALPM_TRANS_FLAG_NODEPS, alpm_trans_prepare, L109 to run the dependency and conflict checks, alpm_trans_commit, L167, an escape hatch alpm_trans_interrupt, L247, and alpm_trans_release, L264. Commit is where the sequencing pays off: for sync operations it loads the package files via _alpm_sync_load (sync.c, L1245), runs pre-transaction hooks at trans.c, L202, then either _alpm_sync_commit (sync.c, L1336) for installs or _alpm_remove_packages, L764 for deletions, and finally post-transaction hooks at trans.c, L238. The queue side is equally plain: alpm_add_pkg, L50 appends a target, and _alpm_upgrade_packages, L678 is the libarchive-driven unpack loop that replaces files one by one.

Verification happens before anything is unpacked. check_validity, L986 inspects each downloaded package’s signature through _alpm_gpgme_checksig, L537, with base64 signature blobs decoded by alpm_decode_signature, L38. A hook is just a parsed .hook file; _alpm_hook_run, L528 matches triggers against the transaction’s file and package lists and shells out only for hooks that actually fired — the mechanism that keeps ldconfig caches and initramfs images fresh without every package carrying install scripts.

Sync repos and sandboxed downloads

A sync database is an archive fetched from a mirror. alpm_db_update, L139 builds one payload per database, attaches a signature request when the configured siglevel includes databases (be_sync.c, L210), and hands the list to the downloader. Package downloads during an upgrade are orchestrated by download_files, L773 after compute_download_size, L310 has already priced the transaction for the confirmation prompt.

The transport is libcurl’s multi interface: curl_set_handle_opts, L374 sets TCP keepalive, a low-speed abort, and resume support per payload, and curl_retry_next_server, L438 transparently walks down the mirror list on failure — the behavior you see as error: failed retrieving file ... Retrying. The distinctive part is who does the downloading: _alpm_use_sandbox, L39 decides whether a root-run pacman should fork a child, alpm_sandbox_setup_child, L51 drops to the SandboxUser account configured in conf.c, L722, the filesystem half restricts writes with _alpm_sandbox_fs_restrict_writes_to, L90, and the syscall half installs a seccomp filter at sandbox_syscalls.c, L136. A malicious mirror thus has a downloaded file and almost no ways to abuse it.

From autotools quirks to a versioned two-artifact build

The build facts in the tree are worth reading on their own. The project builds with meson (meson_version >= 0.61, meson.build, L11) and stamps two distinct versions: pacman itself is 7.1.0 (L3) while the library carries its own ABI version 16.0.1 (L13) — the library is a supported artifact in its own right, and its soname bumps independently of the CLI. The dependency floor is compact: libarchive >= 3.0.0 (L88), libcurl >= 7.55.0 (L97), GPGME >= 1.18.0 (L102), and bash >= 4.4.0 only for the shell completion (L39). Hook files install into libalpm/hooks/ (L71), and because bindings link against the library, alpm.h exposes a capability probe, alpm_capabilities, L2989, reporting ALPM_CAPABILITY_DOWNLOADER and friends so callers can feature-detect at runtime.

Scale-wise, the two halves measure about 16,500 lines of C in lib/libalpm and about 9,400 in src/pacman, with the 2,620-line alpm.h as the contract between them. One quirk worth knowing before you clone: some files like ini.c are git symlinks into a shared src/common/ directory, so a partial checkout can leave you with broken-looking paths. And if you are collecting package-manager designs, the spread is instructive — Homebrew builds everything out of a Ruby class hierarchy (brew), Nix treats the store itself as the source of truth (nix), and pacman keeps the smallest possible trusted core: text files, list scans, and one transaction gate.

Honest Limits

This tour reads master at version 7.1.0, and libalpm’s internal functions — everything prefixed _alpm_ — move without notice between releases; only the alpm_ API in alpm.h is contractual. The makepkg family, including libmakepkg and repo-add, is a separate Bash codebase under scripts/ and was not covered here, so package building and repository creation are out of scope even though they share this repository. The CLI surface also got less attention than it deserves: pacman-conf (src/pacman/pacman-conf.c) is its own tool for querying configuration, and the query, file, and department UI logic in query.c and files.c was skimmed in favor of the engine. Finally, the database format is deliberately undocumented pacman-specific flat files — tools that want to read /var/lib/pacman/local/ must reimplement what be_local.c does, and the signposted way to do that is to link against libalpm instead.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of pacman and libalpm in C: satisfier-based dependency resolution, the flat-file local database, signed sync repos, sandboxed downloads.

entry.title: How pixi Solves Conda and PyPI Environments: A Rust Source Tour

link.title: How pixi Solves Conda and PyPI Environments: A Rust Source Tour

entry.content:
Every data scientist knows the ritual: the notebook works, the handoff does not. Conda environments were supposed to fix “works on my machine,” yet conda env export gives you a YAML file that quietly omits build strings, drifts from what is actually installed, and re-solves differently on every machine. Reproducibility was promised, but what you got was a best-effort recipe.

The second pain is worse. Almost no real project lives in a pure world. You need CUDA-enabled PyTorch from conda-forge because the wheel is enormous and compiler-linked, but you also need a small package that only exists on PyPI. So you run pip inside a conda environment, and now two dependency managers fight over the same site-packages directory — one upgrade silently clobbers the other, and nobody can say which manager owns which file.

pixi is the answer the ecosystem converged on. Written in Rust, it treats both conda and PyPI as first-class sources, resolves them together, and freezes the result into a single pixi.lock — a file you commit, diff in pull requests, and never regenerate by hand. We cloned the repository and read the source. Below are two architecture diagrams generated from the actual tree, followed by a tour of the code paths every claim comes from.

Overview of pixi on branch main: the binary entry, the manifest layer that understands both pixi.toml and pyproject.toml, the solve and lock core, and the install layer that materializes conda packages and PyPI wheels into .pixi environments.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L7 is the binary entrypoint. It immediately spawns a main2 thread with a normalized 2 MB stack, because the default main-thread stack size varies wildly per platform and deep async futures overflow it.
  • execute, L254 parses the clap command line and routes every subcommand — pixi add, pixi run, pixi shell — into the same workspace machinery.
  • PyProjectManifest, L45 is where pyproject.toml support lives: ensure_pixi at line 80 fails with a targeted error if the file exists but has no [tool.pixi] table.
  • Document::kind, L197 abstracts over manifest kind, so pixi add can edit either file format in place with the same code.
  • Workspace, L183 is the central runtime model that joins the parsed manifest with discovered environments.
  • update, L2595 is the orchestrator: it spawns conda solve tasks, then PyPI solve tasks, then writes the lock file.
  • solve_on_blocking_pool, L121 drives the resolvo SAT-style conda solver on a blocking thread pool.
  • resolve_pypi, L334 hands PyPI requirements to a resolver that is not reimplemented — it is uv’s, embedded.
  • PyPIEnvironmentUpdater, L475 applies locked wheels to the prefix, and CondaPrefixUpdater, L170 links conda packages alongside them.

The detail view expands each stage into the real files: manifest deserialization, the lock file engine with satisfiability checks, the command dispatcher that memoizes solves, and the uv-powered PyPI install layer with its conda-clobber detector.

Why the lock file is the product

Open the repository root and the first thing you hit is pixi.lock: 12,944 lines covering five platforms (linux-64, win-64, osx-64, osx-arm64, linux-aarch64). This file is not an export you regenerate — it is the artifact. When you run pixi install, nothing re-solves unless the manifest changed; the code loads the lock and verifies it.

The verification is deliberate and loud. If the lock file on disk was written by a newer pixi, LockFileVersionMismatchError, L127 refuses to continue with “lock-file version is newer than supported” rather than guessing. Before anything is installed, verify_environment_satisfiability, L33 checks that every locked record still matches the manifest: channels, exclude-newer cutoffs, solve strategies, wheel tags. The test suite snapshots dozens of failure cases — mismatch-channel-priority, mismatch-exclude-newer, wheels-with-wrong-tags — each one a real error users hit.

What counts as “out of date” is computed by OutdatedEnvironments, L67. And pixi dogfoods its own medicine: its repository manifest sets [workspace.exclude-newer] with cutoff = "7d" (line 30 of pixi.toml), meaning solves may only consider packages published more than seven days ago. Even the maintainers freeze the future to keep builds reproducible.

One manifest, two ecosystems

The discovery layer is deliberately small. discovery.rs, L448 checks for a pyproject.toml as it walks up the tree, and line 654 shows the pixi.toml counterpart. Both file formats converge on one typed model. PyProjectManifest, L45 reads Python’s standard file and converts it via into_workspace_manifest at line 196, so your [tool.pixi] table becomes the same structure a native pixi.toml produces.

This unification pays off in pixi add and pixi remove. The editable document layer knows which file it is editing — is_pyproject_toml at line 246 of document.rs — and edits that file in place. remove_pypi_dependency at line 340 and add_workspace_dependency at line 499 rewrite the TOML while snapshot tests prove comments and formatting survive. You never hand-edit tables to add a package; the tool does it losslessly.

Dependencies themselves are typed by intent. SpecType, L5 defines Run, Host, and Build — the conda distinction that matters when a package needs a compiler to build but not to run. Conda dependencies and PyPI dependencies live in separate collections (dependencies.rs) but are solved as one coherent environment, which is the whole point.

Solving: resolvo for conda, uv for wheels

The conda side uses resolvo, the Rust solver extracted from mamba, driven on a blocking pool by solve_on_blocking_pool. The lock update orchestrator spawns one task per solve group and platform via spawn_solve_conda_environment_task at line 3276 of update.rs — and orders platforms so the machine you are on solves first, letting prefix work start while other platforms still solve.

Identical environments never solve twice. SolvePixiEnvironmentSpec, L92 canonicalizes everything that affects a solve — channels, priorities, cutoffs, variants — into SolvePixiEnvironmentKey, L183, a cache key the dispatcher memoizes. This is why pixi’s own repo declares solve-group = "python" in nine of its twelve environments: they share one solve result.

There is a subtle glue problem here: a conda package like numpy satisfies a PyPI requirement named numpy, and uv cannot know that. Pixi handles the seam with an explicit conda-to-PyPI name mapping — CondaPypiMapSpec, L399 models the configuration, and the lock updater carries a mapping client (pypi_mapping’s PurlDerivationClient, imported at line 54 of update.rs) so solved conda records are accounted for as if they were installed distributions. Without it, every solve would try to reinstall your conda-provided Python stack from wheels.

The PyPI side is where pixi made its boldest engineering choice: it does not reimplement pip’s resolver. resolve_pypi, L334 plugs pixi’s own provider into the resolver of uv — Astral’s Python package manager. The bridge is visible at resolver_provider.rs, L42, which returns uv_resolver::PackageVersionsResult straight from uv’s types. The uv libraries are compiled into the binary — the workspace Cargo.toml pins uv-distribution-filename = "0.0.99" at line 211 — and the maintainers even keep pixi tasks for switching to a local uv checkout during development. Context for the interpreter comes from UvResolutionContext, L51, built by from_config at line 184, and marker evaluation runs against the conda-installed CPython so sys.platform-style conditions reflect the real environment.

Installation then splits by source. Conda packages are linked by CondaPrefixUpdater::update, L219; wheels go through a planner at planner.rs, L91 that diffs cached, installed, and required distributions, then get_wheel_info, L13 parses .dist-info before linking. And because two managers now share one prefix, pixi added a referee: ClobberReport, L19 detects when a PyPI package is about to overwrite files installed by a conda package and names the collision — capped at five paths per package (line 16) — instead of letting the overwrite happen silently.

From a 2 MB thread stack to 60 crates

pixi is a large, modern Rust workspace: exactly 60 crates under crates/, compiled with edition 2024 (Cargo.toml, L20) and pinned to Rust 1.98.1 in the rust-toolchain file — the same version its own manifest requires via build-variants (>=1.98,<1.99, line 18 of pixi.toml). Version 0.84.2 at the time of writing.

The stack-size story at the top of main.rs is a lesson in itself: Linux gives the main thread 8 MB, Windows only 1 MB, and deeply nested async futures blew the Windows budget. The fix is to spawn a dedicated main2 thread with a RUST_MIN_STACK-overridable size and run the boxed pixi_cli::execute() future there. It is the kind of fix you only write after production crashes.

Cross-platform releases use cargo-zigbuild plus a zig toolchain in the release environment (pixi.toml lines 494–498), and the manifest even declares requires-pixi = ">=0.84.0" — the repository refuses to be managed by an older pixi than its features need. Self-hosting, enforced.

Honest Limits

  • The conda and PyPI worlds still solve as two engines glued at the boundary. Shared markers and extras go through conversion crates (pixi_uv_conversions), which is exactly the kind of seam where exotic edge cases can behave differently than pure-pip or pure-conda setups.
  • pixi.lock at 12,944 lines is machine territory. You commit it, but you do not review it line by line; the meaningful diffs are the manifest changes that forced re-solves.
  • pixi-build — building conda packages from source projects — is still flagged behind preview in pixi’s own manifest (line 14), so that layer is visibly in flux.
  • Each environment materializes its own prefix even inside a solve group; sharing happens at the solve level, not at the hardlink level, so disk usage scales with environment count.
  • This tour covered four of the sixty crates. The task engine, global tool installs (pixi_global), and the PTY layer deserve their own deep dives.
  • One methodological note: the codebase leans hard on snapshot tests — hundreds of .snap files under crates/ pin exact error strings, TOML round-trips, and satisfiability failures. That makes regressions loud, and it is also why the error messages quoted above are stable enough to cite.
entry.summary: Inside prefix-dev/pixi: how the Rust package manager parses pixi.toml and pyproject.toml, solves conda with resolvo and PyPI with uv, and locks it all.

entry.title: pnpm Architecture: How the Content-Addressable Store, Symlinked node_modules, and the Resolver Actually Work

link.title: pnpm Architecture: How the Content-Addressable Store, Symlinked node_modules, and the Resolver Actually Work

entry.content:
Every JavaScript developer knows the ritual: clone a project, run an install, and watch hundreds of megabytes land in node_modules — most of it duplicated bytes that already existed in the project next door. npm and Yarn traditionally solved dependency isolation by copying: every version of every package gets materialized, per project, on your disk. Ten repositories that depend on the same library store ten identical physical copies of it.

The second pain is quieter: phantom dependencies. Flat hoisting — copying every transitive package up to the top-level node_modules so the module resolver can find it — means your code can require() a package you never declared. It works locally and explodes in CI where versions shifted. pnpm’s answer is a stricter layout: only your declared dependencies are visible, and everything else is locked away where Node’s resolution algorithm (we traced that algorithm in the Node.js source) cannot reach it from your project’s root.

The third pain is speed, and it is mostly the first in disguise: installs spend their time re-verifying, re-extracting, and re-writing files already on disk. pnpm’s core bet is that “already installed” should be answerable with a hash lookup and an inode check, not a network round trip and 30,000 file copies. All three answers live in one place: the pnpm monorepo on GitHub. We sparse-checked out its most architecture-revealing packages and read the install machinery end to end. Everything below — every symbol, every line number — was verified against the actual main tree, not against documentation.

pnpm's install at a glance: resolve, store, import, link, hoist. Every node is a real function in the pnpm/pnpm monorepo; every edge is data we traced between them.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • [resolveNpm, L59](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/resolving/npm-resolver/src/resolveNpm.ts#L59) — the resolver entry: pick a registry per scope, try workspace packages, then the lockfile fast path, then the registry.
  • [pickPackageFromMeta, L46](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/resolving/npm-resolver/src/pickPackageFromMeta.ts#L46) — turns a packument into a concrete version, honoring publish-date and deprecated-version policies.
  • [peekLockedPackage, L411](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/resolving/npm-resolver/src/resolveNpm.ts#L411) — the speed trick: when the lockfile pins an integrity-checked tarball, read its manifest straight out of the local store and skip the registry entirely.
  • [createCafs, L94](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/store/cafs/src/index.ts#L94) — builds the content-addressable file store API: every blob addressed by its sha512 digest.
  • [contentPathFromHex, L21](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/store/cafs/src/getFilePathInCafs.ts#L21) — maps a digest to files/<2 chars>/<rest>, with an -exec suffix for executable files.
  • [writeBufferToCafs, L12](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/store/cafs/src/writeBufferToCafs.ts#L12) — exclusive-create blob writes so concurrent installs cannot clobber each other, plus in-place repair of corrupt blobs.
  • [createIndexedPkgImporter, L27](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/fs/indexed-pkg-importer/src/index.ts#L27) — chooses how files leave the store: reflink clone, hardlink, or copy; auto probes and remembers the winner.
  • [linkDirectDeps, L30](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/installing/linking/direct-dep-linker/src/linkDirectDeps.ts#L30) — symlinks each project’s direct dependencies into its node_modules.
  • [hoist, L40](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/installing/linking/hoist/src/index.ts#L40) — the optional, opt-in hoister for packages that genuinely need loose resolution.

The detail view: 34 functions across six groups. Follow the edges from resolver to store, store to importer, importer to linker, linker to hoister.

The Content-Addressable Store: sha512, Two-Character Fan-Out

When a tarball arrives, pnpm does not unpack it into node_modules. It walks every file, hashes it, and writes it into a machine-wide store under a path derived from that hash. The algorithm is not configurable at this layer: HASH_ALGORITHM (L38) is exported as a plain 'sha512', and addBufferToCafs (L129) computes the digest with crypto.hash(HASH_ALGORITHM, buffer, 'hex'). A comment right above it is refreshingly empirical: “Calculating the integrity of the file is surprisingly fast. 30K files are calculated in 1 second. Hence, from a performance perspective, there is no win in fetching the package index file from the registry.”

The address layout is a two-level fan-out: contentPathFromHex (L25) builds files/<first two hex chars>/<remaining chars>, and appends -exec when the file is executable — decided by modeIsExecutable (L8), a one-liner testing (mode & 0o111) !== 0. That split exists because hard links preserve the store file’s mode, so executables and non-executables must be physically distinct blobs. The same function carries a micro-optimization comment worth quoting: the path is built with template strings instead of path.join because it is “a hot path called ~30k times per cold install; avoiding path.join saves ~30ms per install.”

The write path is defensive in an instructive way. writeBufferToCafs (L12) keeps a per-path locker, then uses exclusive creation — writeFileExclusive (L30) opens with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, so if another process created the same content-addressed file concurrently, you get EEXIST rather than a silent overwrite. The EEXIST winner then verifies the file’s integrity instead of trusting it. And if an existing blob fails verification (a crash mid-write, disk corruption), overwriteFileInPlace (L139) truncates and rewrites the file under the same inode — the comment cites issue pnpm/pnpm#3445 and explains why: every hard link from every project’s node_modules shares that inode, so one in-place repair heals all of them at once. Temporary files are named with the process ID plus worker thread ID (pathTemp, L235) instead of random bytes.

From Store to node_modules: Clone, Hardlink, Copy

The store lives once per machine; node_modules is a projection of it. The projection is built by the indexed package importer, and the strategy is explicit: PackageImportMethod (L21) is the union 'auto' | 'hardlink' | 'copy' | 'clone' | 'clone-or-copy', defaulting to auto in the switch at L45. auto probes the filesystem: it tries a reflink clone first (createClonePkg, L193 uses the @reflink/reflink native addon on macOS and Windows, and COPYFILE_FICLONE_FORCE on Linux), then a hardlink, and falls back to copying — caching whichever strategy won so later packages skip the probing.

The workhorse is linkOrCopy (L345): a plain fs.linkSync per file, where EEXIST is treated as success, and a curious fallback comment admits that “in some VERY rare cases (1 in a thousand), hard-link creation fails on Windows” — so the code simply copies instead. Before linking at all, pkgLinkedToStore (L392) compares inode numbers between the target file and the store file: equal ino means the hard link already exists and the whole package import can be skipped. That single stats0.ino === stats1.ino check is why repeated installs are nearly free.

Whole-directory safety is handled by importIndexedDir (L67): try an exclusive mkdir and import straight into it; if it exists, build the package in a staging directory and commit it with an atomic rename (importWithStaging, L87). One subtle ordering rule: package.json is imported last, through the atomic importer, because a concurrent reader uses its presence as the completion marker.

Symlinks All the Way Down: The node_modules Layout

This is the part users actually see. Your node_modules/react is not a directory — it is a symlink into node_modules/.pnpm/react@19.1.0/node_modules/react, and the files inside that are hard links into the store. The symlink itself is created by symlinkDependency (L10), which calls symlinkDir after joining the alias into the modules directory. The direct-dep linker linkDirectDeps (L30) runs it for every workspace project and dedupes: a dependency already linked from the root is unlinked from sub-projects rather than duplicated (linkDirectDepsAndDedupe, L43).

Because only declared dependencies get a top-level symlink, undeclared transitive packages are invisible to your code — phantom dependencies are structurally impossible, not just discouraged. For teams that still need loose resolution, hoisting exists as an explicit opt-in. hoist (L40) walks the dependency graph (graphWalker, L5), sorts candidates by depth (hoistGraph, L238), and lets the first claimant win each alias. selectHoistedModulesDir (L8) shows the two destinations: private hoists go to node_modules/.pnpm/node_modules (visible to nested packages, not to your source), while public hoists land in node_modules itself. A newer option, virtualStoreType: global, goes further: one virtual store shared across projects, per the repo’s own docs.

One implementation note: pnpm itself is written in TypeScript; for the tooling side, see our TypeScript compiler internals tour.

The Resolver: From Specifier to Tarball

Everything above assumes pnpm already knows which version to install. Deciding that is the resolver’s job, and its first move is avoiding work. resolveNpm (L59) handles workspace: protocol specifiers before touching the network (L106), then the fast path at peekLockedPackageUnlessUpdating (L158) checks whether the lockfile’s current resolution is an integrity-pinned tarball; if so, peekLockedPackage (L411) reads the manifest from the local store.
