The comment above it explains the win plainly: “This avoids the expensive metadata fetch from the registry.”

When a registry fetch is unavoidable, pickPackageFromMeta (L46) applies the policies: it detects unpublished packages (UNPUBLISHED_PKG, L64), rejects metadata whose name mismatches the request, and delegates range resolution to pickVersionByVersionRange (L222), which prefers dist-tags.latest and deliberately uses loose semver so a * range can still match prerelease versions — the comment cites issue #865. Deprecated versions get one more chance at redemption: nonDeprecatedPick (L349) tries the same release line for a non-deprecated alternative before giving up. If nothing matches, NoMatchingVersionError (L11) surfaces the failure when neither the registry nor the workspace has a match.

From Copying Every File to Linking Once: Engineering Facts Worth Stealing

The repo’s own shape encodes its history. The TypeScript CLI and roughly sixty library packages live under pnpm11/, and pnpm-workspace.yaml documents a versioning band: while the CLI is on major 11, every library rides majors 1100–1199, bumped in lockstep so a consumer never mixes incompatible internals. STORE_VERSION is pinned to 'v11' at L9 of core/constants — store layouts change with majors, and the version suffix keeps an old binary from reading a store format it cannot parse. The default store path is <pnpm-home>/store/v11, but pnpm11/store/path probes the project’s drive first and falls back to <mountpoint>/.pnpm-store/v11, because hard links cannot cross volumes. And the story no longer ends at TypeScript: the same workspace file notes that the published npm pnpm package is now fronted by a thin Rust wrapper (the workspace package pacquet) that dispatches to per-platform binaries — a good segue into our Rust source tour.

The micro-decisions are just as transferable. Path construction in the store’s hottest function is hand-inlined to save ~30 ms per cold install. Hashing is trusted over network metadata because it measured faster. Temp files encode pid plus worker-thread ID instead of random bytes. Integrity verification runs in worker threads, with per-worker tallies handed back and summed by the main thread (the comment at L36 of checkPkgFilesIntegrity). None of these are glamorous; together they are why a warm install of thousands of packages finishes in seconds.

Honest Limits

This tour reads four packages deeply — store/cafs, fs/indexed-pkg-importer, resolving/npm-resolver, and installing/linking — out of a workspace listing dozens more under pnpm11/. The Rust wrapper (pacquet) and the pnpr experiment were not audited; statements about them come from pnpm-workspace.yaml comments, not their code. Line numbers refer to main as of today and will drift. Most diagram edges are direct calls, but a few (notably “blobs ready to import”) represent data flow between install stages rather than literal invocations. On exotic filesystems the code carries the most fallback comments; treat any single observed behavior as one branch of a larger decision tree.
entry.summary: How pnpm works under the hood: a sha512 content-addressable store, hard links into node_modules/.pnpm, strict symlinks, and the npm resolver, read from source.

entry.title: How Scoop Works: Manifests, Shims, and Buckets Inside the PowerShell Source

link.title: How Scoop Works: Manifests, Shims, and Buckets Inside the PowerShell Source

entry.content:
On a fresh Windows machine, installing three CLI tools usually means three graphical wizards, three Start Menu entries, one or two “do you want to allow this app to make changes” prompts, and a PATH variable you edit by hand through a dialog buried in System Properties. Six months later you uninstall one of them, and the registry keeps half of it forever. Scoop, the command-line installer maintained as ScoopInstaller/Scoop, flips that experience: you type scoop install ripgrep, it fetches a portable archive, unpacks it under a single user-writable root, and drops a tiny launcher onto your PATH. No wizard, no admin prompt, no registry keys.

The second pain point is the one Scoop is really about: PATH management. Every Windows developer has installed a tool, opened a new terminal, typed the command, and gotten “not recognized” because the installer appended a directory that the current shell never re-read. Scoop solves this once, globally, with one directory of generated launchers called shims. Everything it installs becomes reachable through that one directory, so the PATH never grows per-app.

This post reads the actual source on the master branch — not the documentation. The repository is pure PowerShell: 19 helper files under lib/, 28 command scripts under libexec/, and a core.ps1 that alone runs 1,395 lines. If you know /brew/, Scoop is the closest spiritual equivalent on Windows, but with a crucial difference: where Homebrew builds from formulas, Scoop installs prebuilt portable archives, and where /winget/ wraps vendor installers, Scoop’s default buckets contain apps that need no installer at all. Two generated diagrams below map the real call graph; every symbol and line number in this article was checked against the tree.

Figure 1 — Scoop at the module level: a 48-line entry script dispatches into 28 libexec commands, which lean on five lib helpers for manifests, downloads, extraction, shims, and buckets, all constrained by schema.json.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • install_app, L8 — the orchestrator; lines 9 through 81 run manifest resolution, download, extraction, shimming, and persistence in that exact order.
  • Get-Manifest, L34 — turns an app name into a manifest object, trying buckets, URLs, and user manifests in sequence.
  • Invoke-ScoopDownload, L5 — the cache-aware downloader; check_hash, L728 verifies hashes before anything executes.
  • Invoke-Extraction, L3 — routes archives to five expanders covering zip, 7z, MSI, Inno Setup, and WiX dark payloads.
  • shim, L949 — writes the .exe plus .shim launcher pair that makes every tool reachable from any shell.
  • command_files, L5 — discovers commands by listing libexec and the shims directory for scoop-*.ps1 files.
  • Find-BucketDirectory, L3 — a bucket is just a folder of JSON manifests on disk, usually a git checkout.
  • update, L261 — re-resolves the manifest for each installed app and reuses the same download-and-install path.
  • Find-ScoopDBItem, L262 — an optional SQLite cache that makes scoop search instant across all buckets.

Figure 2 — The detailed graph: how bin/scoop.ps1, the dispatch layer, 28 libexec commands, the install runtime, the manifest layer, and storage (core, database, buckets) connect.

The dispatcher: one switch, 28 commands

Everything starts in bin/scoop.ps1, and the file is astonishingly small: 48 lines, with #Requires -Version 5 on line 1. Lines 4 through 7 dot-source exactly four libraries — core.ps1, buckets.ps1, commands.ps1, and help.ps1 — and line 9 reads $Args[0] into $subCommand. A single switch then matches that word against the list produced by commands and calls exec.

The discovery mechanism in lib/commands.ps1 is the design decision worth stealing. command_files (line 5) lists two directories — libexec and the user’s $scoopdir\shims — and keeps anything matching scoop-.*?\.ps1$. command_name (line 14) strips the prefix, and command_path (line 18) resolves a command either to a built-in script or, failing that, to the shim script with the same name. exec (line 35) invokes it with splatted arguments. The consequence: adding a Scoop command is nothing more than dropping a scoop-<name>.ps1 file into libexec, and third-party aliases work the same way — add_alias (line 43) writes a one-line script into the shims directory. Today there are 28 commands, from scoop-install.ps1 to scoop-virustotal.ps1, and none of them are registered anywhere: existence of the file is the registration.

install_app: the nine-step install loop

libexec/scoop-install.ps1 parses flags with getopt (line 46, options giksua:), then expands the app list with dependencies via Get-Dependency (line 130, defined in lib/depends.ps1:1), prunes already-installed apps (line 134), and loops install_app over whatever remains (line 148).

The loop body is the whole product. install_app first calls Get-Manifest (line 9), validates the version string (lines 15-19), and resolves the architecture with Get-SupportedArchitecture (line 165 in lib/manifest.ps1), which understands 32bit, 64bit, and arm64. Then the sequence at lines 48 through 73: versiondir (line 48) computes apps\<app>\<version>; Invoke-ScoopDownload (line 52) fetches into a shared cache; Invoke-Extraction (line 53) unpacks it; Invoke-Installer (line 56) runs an embedded installer only if the manifest declares one; link_current (line 58) repoints a current directory junction at the new version folder — the function at line 234 creates that junction and honors a NO_JUNCTION config opt-out; create_shims (line 59); Start Menu shortcuts (line 60); env_add_path (line 62); and persist_data (line 66) moves stateful folders into persist\<app> so version upgrades never wipe your data. Finally save_installed_manifest (line 72) records what was installed so uninstall and update can reverse the process cleanly.

Shims: how portable apps end up on PATH

A shim is Scoop’s answer to the Windows PATH problem, and it is implemented in one function: shim in lib/core.ps1 at line 949. The first thing it does is Add-Path (line 952) on the shims directory — the only PATH entry Scoop ever needs, and it is managed by Add-Path and Remove-Path in lib/system.ps1 (lines 96 and 122).

For an .exe target, Scoop copies a prebuilt launcher binary from supporting/shims/ — get_shim_path (line 1120) selects among three shipped variants (kiennq by default, plus scoopcs and 71) according to the SHIM config — and writes a sibling .shim file containing path = "..." (line 987). It even checks the PE header of the target with Get-PESubsystem (line 1 of the same file) and patches the launcher to be a GUI binary when the target is one (lines 992-997). Batch files get a wrapper .cmd plus a POSIX sh script (lines 998-1011), and PowerShell scripts get a .ps1 shim (line 1012). Conflicts are not silent: warn_on_overwrite (line 930) tells you when an existing shim would be clobbered. The net effect is that tools\ never needs to be on your PATH — only the single shims directory does.

Buckets: when the app catalog is a git repo

Scoop’s catalogs are called buckets, and they are literally git repositories full of JSON manifests. buckets.json at the repo root names ten known ones: main, extras, versions, nirsoft, sysinternals, php, nerd-fonts, nonportable, java, and games. known_bucket_repos (line 37 in lib/buckets.ps1) reads that file, add_bucket (line 123) clones a new one with Invoke-Git (line 237 in lib/core.ps1), and Find-AppBucket (line 100 in lib/manifest.ps1) scans buckets to resolve a bare app name. The whole catalog layer is /git/ underneath — scoop update runs Sync-Scoop (line 64 of libexec/scoop-update.ps1) to pull Scoop itself and Sync-Bucket (line 155) to pull every bucket, and old versions stay installable because Find-HistoricalManifest (line 277) can dig a manifest out of the bucket’s git history.

Manifest shape is enforced by schema.json, a 22.9 KB JSON Schema draft-07 document with additionalProperties: false at line 4. Only three top-level fields are required (lines 678-682): version, homepage, and license. The hash grammar at line 7 accepts raw SHA-256 or prefixed sha1|sha256|sha512|md5 values. Keeping those manifests fresh is bucket-side tooling: lib/autoupdate.ps1 implements URL scraping with find_hash_in_textfile (line 43), find_hash_in_json (line 114), and find_hash_in_xml (line 148), all driven by Invoke-AutoUpdate (line 474) — that is the engine behind the checkver field maintainers put in every manifest.

From a two-line bootstrap to a 1,395-line core.ps1: build facts

The installer’s own bootstrap, bin/install.ps1, is two lines: #Requires -Version 5 and Invoke-RestMethod https://get.scoop.sh | Invoke-Expression. Everything downstream is plain script. Here are the engineering facts that stood out while reading the tree:

  • There is no compiled Scoop code. The only binaries shipped in-repo are the three shim launcher builds under supporting/shims/, each with a checksum file beside it, plus a small C# manifest validator under supporting/validator/ that checks manifests against schema.json.
  • lib/ contains 19 files and libexec/ 28; lib/core.ps1 is the largest at 1,395 lines, holding config, path layout (lines 366-388: basedir, appsdir, shimdir, persistdir), process helpers, and the git wrapper.
  • Search can be backed by SQLite, but only if you opt in. Flipping the use_sqlite_cache config triggers Set-ScoopDB from lib/core.ps1 lines 229-234; Get-SQLite (line 18 of lib/database.ps1) downloads the System.Data.SQLite driver on demand, and Open-ScoopDB (line 75) creates the app table (line 93). Without it, scoop search falls back to a regex scan, matching names, binaries, and shortcuts (line 185 of libexec/scoop-search.ps1).
  • Self-update is time-based, not version-based: is_scoop_outdated (line 1251 of lib/core.ps1) returns true when the LAST_UPDATE config is more than 3 hours old.
  • External helpers are resolved through Get-HelperPath (line 476 of lib/core.ps1), which prefers Scoop’s own git (mingw64\bin\git.exe, line 491) before falling back to PATH, and knows 7zip, lessmsi, innounp, WiX dark, and aria2. Aria2 acceleration is entirely optional — Test-Aria2Enabled (line 262 of lib/download.ps1) gates it at runtime.
  • Downloads are hash-checked by default; check_hash (line 728 of lib/download.ps1) fails the install on mismatch rather than warning.

Honest Limits

Scoop is deliberately narrow, and knowing the boundaries saves time. It is Windows-only and requires PowerShell 5; it refuses to do services, drivers, or anything needing machine-wide registration — that is why the nonportable bucket exists, and it warns before running those installers. Hash checks only protect you as far as the manifest author: the URL list comes from buckets, and when a vendor moves a file, installs break until someone updates the manifest — github_ratelimit_reached (line 593 of lib/download.ps1) is a reminder that even API metadata has quotas. The SQLite search index is opt-in, so out of the box, searching large buckets means scanning JSON files. Shims can shadow same-named executables from other directories; warn_on_overwrite mitigates but does not prevent it. And compared with /winget/, which drives vendor installers and the Microsoft Store, Scoop covers a smaller catalog but gives you clean, scriptable, user-scoped installs with real uninstall semantics. For anything on the default buckets, it remains the calmest way to keep a Windows development machine tidy — and after reading this source, you can trace every step of that calm from a 48-line dispatcher down to a junction repoint.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of ScoopInstaller/Scoop: how manifests, shims, buckets, and 28 PowerShell commands install portable Windows apps without MSI clutter.

entry.title: How uv Works: The Rust Architecture Behind Python’s Fastest Package Manager

link.title: How uv Works: The Rust Architecture Behind Python’s Fastest Package Manager

entry.content:
Every Python developer knows the ritual: create a virtualenv, upgrade pip, run pip install -r requirements.txt, then stare at the resolver as it backtracks through incompatible version combinations of your transitive dependencies. On projects with deep graphs — a data stack pulling in dozens of packages — resolution alone can stall for minutes, and none of that work is reused between runs. The cache misses, the wheels download again, and the interpreter churns through a parser built for a world where networks were slow.

uv is Astral’s answer to exactly this pain. It replaces the pip workflow — install, compile, sync, lock — with a single Rust binary that treats dependency resolution as a concurrent systems problem rather than a sequential script. Since its release it has spread rapidly through the Python ecosystem, and teams that adopted it mostly stayed: the speed is not a marketing veneer, it is structural, coming from how the resolver, the cache, and the installer are designed at the source level.

This post is a source-level tour of that design. We cloned the repository at commit 7f396534d583 on main and read the real code — every symbol and line number below is checked against the actual tree, not guessed. If you like Rust systems archaeology in the same spirit as ripgrep, this is a good one to follow along in a second terminal window.

uv's architecture on main: the CLI drives workspace discovery, a PubGrub resolver fed by an async registry client, and a planner that installs through the shared cache.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Resolver::resolve, L314 — the entry point that pairs a metadata-fetching future with the solver and joins them via tokio::try_join! (L344).
  • ResolverState, L131 — the shared state read by the solver, the fetcher, and the reporter.
  • MetadataRequests, L22 — metadata requests queued through an mpsc::channel(300) (resolver/mod.rs L321), sized deliberately to accommodate batch prefetching.
  • BatchPrefetcher, L44 — predicts which metadata the solver will need next and fetches it in batches before it is asked for.
  • PrioritizedDist, L26 — ranks compatible wheels and source distributions per version, including platform tag priority.
  • Cache, L162 — a versioned bucket layout (CacheBucket, L1042) with pruning that is hardlink-aware (L623).
  • CachedClient, L216 — wraps BaseClient and deserializes cached metadata zero-copy through the rkyv helpers in rkyvutil.rs (L25).
  • Lock, L313 — the lockfile writer, with format version 1 (L99) and revision 5 (L133) constants guarding compatibility.
  • create_venv, L81 — the tail of every install: write pyvenv.cfg, seed it, and link the environment.

The full resolution path in detail: request channel, prefetcher, fork handling, rkyv-backed cache layers, and the installer's link modes.

A Workspace of 91 Crates

uv is not one big Rust file; it is a disciplined Cargo workspace. The root Cargo.toml declares members = ["crates/*"] (L2) — which resolves to 91 crate directories — with resolver = "2" (L8), edition = "2024" (L11), and rust-version = "1.98.0" (L12). Exactly one crate, uv-trampoline, is excluded because it needs nightly (L6); it builds the tiny Windows launcher executables instead of relying on batch-script entry points.

The layering is strict. The uv binary crate contains only pub async fn run (crates/uv/src/lib.rs L134) and an unsafe fn main (L3077); the actual command tree lives in uv-cli, where Cli (L84), Commands (L345), and PipCommand (L788) are defined with clap. Settings are parsed into typed option structs — ResolverOptions (crates/uv-settings/src/settings.rs L662) and InstallerOptions (L561) — rather than passed around as loose config blobs.

The small crates at the bottom of the graph are where performance habits show. uv-performance-memory-allocator switches the global allocator to mimalloc on Windows and jemalloc elsewhere, selected per target architecture (lib.rs L1-L19). uv-small-str defines SmallString(ArcStr) (L10), a compact string representation for the millions of package names and versions flowing through a solve. uv-fastid generates identifiers as a raw Id([u8; 16]) (L20) instead of heap-allocated UUID strings. None of these are glamorous, but together they cut allocation churn from the hot path.

The Resolver: PubGrub on a Dedicated Thread

The heart of uv is crates/uv-resolver. The Resolver generic struct (L124) carries two pluggable pieces — a ResolverProvider for metadata and an InstalledPackagesProvider for the current environment — while ResolverState (L131) holds everything mutable. When resolve starts, it does something unusual: it spawns the PubGrub solver on a dedicated OS thread explicitly named uv-resolver (L328-L333) and runs the metadata fetcher as an async task concurrently, joining both with try_join!. Solving is CPU-bound pointer chasing; fetching is IO-bound. Separating them means neither starves the other.

The solver itself is not a hand-rolled SAT search. uv imports a fork of the PubGrub crate — the workspace pins pubgrub 0.7.1 as the package astral-pubgrub with an unstable-state-api feature (Cargo.toml L229) — and adapts it through UvDependencyProvider (dependency_provider.rs L15). Inside solve (L353) you can see the machinery: a FxHashSet of visited packages (L366), State::init of the PubGrub machine (L369), a BatchPrefetcher (L370), and a ForkState whose incompatibility arena is taken out and reused across branches (L378). Forks — uv’s mechanism for branching the solve when a package needs contradictory versions — are tracked in ForkMap (fork_map.rs L16), a plain FxHashMap<PackageName, Vec<Entry<T>>> with a unit-typed ForkSet alias (L12).

Selection policy is separated from the search. VersionMap (version_map.rs L34) decides which versions are candidates for a package given the Python target; PrioritizedDist (prioritized_distribution.rs L26) ranks the compatible wheels and sdists within a version, with a wheel-compatibility variant carrying an explicit tag priority (L460-L493); and AllowedYanks (yanks.rs L14) encodes whether yanked releases may still be selected. This separation is what lets uv implement resolution modes and preferences without tangling them into the solver.

The Cache: Hardlink-Aware and Zero-Copy

uv’s cache is the reason a second sync feels instantaneous. Cache (crates/uv-cache/src/lib.rs L162) organizes disk under versioned CacheBucket directories (L1042) — the doc comments show concrete layouts like wheel-metadata-v0/pypi/foo/foo-1.0.0-py3-none-any.msgpack — so a cache format change invalidates only one bucket instead of everything. The prune logic is unusually careful: “Remove file objects with no hardlinks outside the files bucket” (L623-L626), counting references with uv_fs::hardlink_count (L640) before deleting, because installed environments may still point into the cache.

Networking goes through RegistryClient (crates/uv-client/src/registry_client.rs L275), whose simple_detail (L403) fetches PyPI Simple API index pages, built on BaseClient (base_client.rs L766) configured by BaseClientBuilder (L109) for retries, proxies, and TLS. Cached responses are handled by CachedClient — literally a one-field tuple struct around BaseClient (L216) — whose Cacheable trait supports both serde and rkyv (L30-L38). The rkyv path is the interesting one: rkyvutil.rs defines the Serializer (L25) and Deserializer (L36) aliases so cached metadata can be read without deserializing into owned Rust types. On top of that sits a real HTTP caching layer implementing RFC 9111 semantics — revalidation (httpcache/mod.rs L386), Vary handling (L192) — and when a project lacks PEP 658 metadata files, uv falls back to reading metadata from remote zip central directories (wheel_metadata_from_remote_zip, remote_metadata.rs L49). Credentials are memoized in CredentialsCache (crates/uv-auth/src/cache.rs L35).

From Backtracking to Batch Prefetch: Build Facts in Numbers

A few concrete engineering facts from the tree, for readers who like numbers:

  • The metadata channel between fetcher and solver is mpsc::channel(300) — the comment (resolver/mod.rs L320) says the size is set large specifically to accommodate batch prefetching. Prefetching exists because PubGrub explores in a breadth-ish order the fetcher cannot predict one request at a time.
  • The lockfile format is version 1 with revision 5 (const VERSION, L99; const REVISION, L133 in lock/mod.rs), and the revision history is documented in place (L126-L132): revision 2 added upload times, 3 added per-package exclude-newer, 5 added default-group metadata. Older files with revision = 3 still read correctly.
  • LinkMode (crates/uv-fs/src/link.rs L26) has exactly four variants — Clone, Copy, Hardlink, Symlink — and the default is Clone on macOS and Linux (APFS, btrfs, xfs, bcachefs support copy-on-write) and Hardlink elsewhere (L15-L17, L39-L51). Installs are therefore usually reflinks or hardlinks into cache-owned files, not byte copies.
  • The install planner, Planner::build (crates/uv-installer/src/plan.rs L291), partitions work into cached distributions, remote downloads, and reinstalls (see the pushes at L419, L453, L462), and Installer::install (installer.rs L102) has a synchronous twin install_blocking (L146).
  • Interpreter discovery — how uv finds the CPython interpreters it will build environments on, including its own managed downloads — lives in find_python_installations (crates/uv-python-discovery/src/discovery.rs L922), with the resulting Interpreter value modeled in uv-python-interpreter (interpreter.rs L51).

Installs, LinkMode, and Virtualenvs

Once the plan exists, the installer walks it. Cached distributions are materialized through install_wheel (crates/uv-install-wheel/src/install.rs L53), which unpacks wheel payloads into site-packages using uv-fs (declared as a workspace dependency in uv-install-wheel’s Cargo.toml, L24) — that is where LinkMode actually gets exercised file by file. Environment creation is create_venv (crates/uv-virtualenv/src/lib.rs L81), which writes pyvenv.cfg, records a seed setting (virtualenv.rs L580-L582, with the Seed enum at L731), and on Windows installs trampoline executables instead of Python-script launchers (L294). Workspaces — uv’s monorepo feature — are discovered by walking upward through pyproject.toml files, a procedure documented step by step above Workspace::discover (crates/uv-workspace/src/workspace.rs L447-L463), with a dedicated WorkspaceCache so repeated discovery does not re-read every member manifest (L152-L160).

Honest Limits

This is a static source tour, not a benchmark: we verified structures, algorithms, and constants in the tree at commit 7f396534d583, but no end-to-end timings were measured for this post, and uv’s own performance claims live in its benchmarks documents rather than in code. Line numbers will drift as main moves — the resolver file alone is several thousand lines and changes weekly. The diagrams necessarily flatten nuance: pubgrub/mod.rs is a thin re-export module over Astral’s forked crate, and the fork/arena logic inside resolver/mod.rs spans thousands of lines we compressed into two nodes. Finally, uv is moving fast — the lockfile revision, the resolver’s fork machinery, and the workspace discovery rules have all changed in recent months, so treat this as a snapshot of a healthy, actively evolving codebase, not a frozen specification.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of uv: the PubGrub resolver, rkyv-backed cache, hardlink installs, and virtualenv engine that make Python packaging fast.

entry.title: How winget Works: A C++ Source Tour of Microsoft’s Windows Package Manager

link.title: How winget Works: A C++ Source Tour of Microsoft’s Windows Package Manager

entry.content:
Installing software on Windows has been a small act of faith for decades: search the web, download an exe from wherever the results point, hope it is clean, click Next until the wizard releases you. Automating that ritual was worse. Every MSI had its own silent flags, every EXE ignored conventions, and every deployment script quietly depended on one machine’s quirks. Windows Package Manager took that pain seriously: one client, winget, ships with Windows 11 and Windows 10, reads a declarative manifest instead of a web page, and installs, upgrades, and uninstalls from a single quiet command that can be scripted end to end.

The client is not a script wrapper around msiexec. microsoft/winget-cli is native C++ and the four projects that carry the product are substantial: AppInstallerCLICore, AppInstallerCommonCore, AppInstallerRepositoryCore, and AppInstallerSharedLib together hold roughly 103,000 lines of C++ across 622 .cpp and .h files. The design makes commands deliberately thin. Almost every interesting decision - which source to query, which installer applies to this machine, whether the downloaded file is trustworthy - happens in workflow tasks and repository sources that commands compose with a streaming operator.

This post follows one package from argv to an installed program, using the actual tree on branch master: where arguments land, how a search becomes a SQL query, how a YAML manifest is narrowed down to exactly one installer, and what happens between the download and the first process spawn. Both diagrams below were generated from the real repository structure, and every code link points at the exact line it cites.

Overview: from wmain through the command layer and the workflow engine, out to the composite sources and the SQLite index, and down into the install chain.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • wmain, L7 is barely ten lines. The winget exe shim immediately calls WindowsPackageManagerCLIMain, an export declared in WindowsPackageManager.h and listed in Source.def - the CLI already lives inside a DLL that COM clients can load too.
  • CoreMain, L168 registers a shutdown blocker so Windows Update cannot kill a mid-flight install, installs a SIGABRT handler, initializes the COM apartment, and only then dispatches into the command tree.
  • RootCommand::GetCommands, L177 is the honest table of contents: 24 always-on commands, from install, show, search, upgrade, and uninstall to pin, configure, download, dsc, and even mcp.
  • SearchCommand::ExecuteInternal, L78 reads like a sentence: OpenSource() followed by SearchSourceForMany followed by HandleSearchResultFailures.
  • InstallCommand::ExecuteInternal, L120 splits the world in two: a –manifest argument goes straight to GetManifestFromArg, while everything else opens the default composite source and resolves a package id.
  • InstallOrUpgradeSinglePackage, L390 is the shared install/upgrade spine: SearchSourceForSingle, version selection, then the single-package chain.
  • InstallSinglePackage, L663 states the whole install contract in a dozen lines: prompts, dependency installation, the download, execution, and registration for after-reboot completion.
  • SQLiteIndex::Search, L315 is where “search” stops being marketing and becomes SQL over the locally downloaded catalog index.

Detail: the same flow with every factory, schema version, and verification step the CLI touches on the way to a silent install.

One entry point, 24 commands, and one operator

The exe is a shim, and that is a deliberate architectural fact. src/AppInstallerCLI/main.cpp forwards to WindowsPackageManagerCLIMain, which the WindowsPackageManager project exports through Source.def. The same DLL also builds the out-of-proc COM classes - PackageManager, FindPackagesOptions, InstallOptions and friends are registered with WRL creator maps in src/WindowsPackageManager/main.cpp. That is how the PowerShell module and other automation clients reach the same engine the console does, without reimplementing any of it.

Inside the CLI, a command is little more than a workflow expression. The carrier is Execution::Context, defined in src/AppInstallerCLICore/ExecutionContext.h as an EnumBasedVariantMap of typed data slots that also implements ICancellable. Arguments enter as typed slots, search results, selected installers, and download results pass through the same map, and flags like ShowSearchResultsOnPartialFailure tune behavior without new parameters.

The composition operator is the actual engine. The operator overload at WorkflowBase.cpp, L1907 executes one WorkflowTask and then checks whether the context now holds a termination error; the first failure short-circuits everything downstream. There is no scheduler in the console path, just composed function calls with early exits. Parallelism exists where the COM server needs it: ContextOrchestrator sizes its per-command queues from std::thread::hardware_concurrency() (ContextOrchestrator.cpp, L51), so server-side callers can run more than one operation at a time.

One index, many sources

winget’s default catalog is not GitHub at runtime. SourceList.cpp pins the two built-ins: the winget source at https://cdn.winget.microsoft.com/cache (SourceList.cpp, L41) and the msstore source at https://storeedgefd.dsx.mp.microsoft.com/v9.0 (L65). CreateSourceFromDetails in RepositorySource.cpp (L34) maps each SourceDetails to a concrete factory: the winget catalog arrives as a locally cached SQLite database, while msstore is a REST service with its own versioned response schema under Rest/Schema (1.0 through 1.28).

The SQLite side is the interesting half for a source diver. SQLiteIndexSource wraps the index in the ISource contract and forwards SearchRequest objects to SQLiteIndex::Search. A request carries field-value pairs with a MatchType, and RepositorySearch.cpp (L175) enumerates the whole vocabulary: Exact, CaseInsensitive, StartsWith, Substring, Wildcard, Fuzzy, and FuzzySubstring. That range explains why winget search visual finds things winget search VisualStudio would miss.

When install or upgrade needs both catalogs plus the machine’s installed programs, OpenCompositeSource builds a CompositeSource. Its Search (CompositeSource.cpp, L1415) fans the request out over every inner source, merges results, and correlates them against installed packages using the ARP (Add/Remove Programs) correlation in ARPCorrelation.cpp - the mechanism that decides “this available package is the thing already on your machine”.

Manifests: YAML in, exactly one installer out

Every package in the winget catalog is described by YAML manifests in the community winget-pkgs repository: an installer file with URLs, hashes, and switches, plus locale and version documents. The client parses them with a libyaml-backed parser - vcpkg.json lists libyaml as a dependency - through Manifest::ParseManifest in src/AppInstallerCommonCore/Manifest/YamlParser.cpp (L585). The ManifestYamlPopulator turns the parsed document tree into the Manifest struct.

Choosing the installer is where winget earns its keep on real machines. ManifestComparator::GetPreferredInstaller (ManifestComparator.cpp, L782) first applies filters that eliminate inapplicable candidates, then orders what remains with comparators for machine architecture, installer type, installed type, scope, and locale - the Create() calls live at lines 83, 218, 338, 405, 449, and 545 of the same file. The winner must still survive EnsureApplicableInstaller (InstallFlow.cpp, L303) before anything is allowed to run. If you have ever wondered why winget picked the x64 inno installer instead of the x86 msi on your box, that file is the answer.

The last mile: download, verify, execute

The install chain is the part users actually feel, and it is full of small, defensible engineering choices. DownloadInstaller (DownloadFlow.cpp, L275) does not blindly re-fetch: it first calls ExistingInstallerFileHasHashMatch (L194), which hashes the previously downloaded file and compares it with the expected buffer, so an interrupted-then-retried install can reuse a fully verified file. Fresh downloads even use the installer’s SHA256 as the download identifier (L404-405), which makes the cache key self-describing.

Verification is a hard gate, not a checkbox. VerifyInstallerHash (L542) compares the digest computed over the downloaded bytes with the hash recorded in the manifest, and a mismatch is fatal unless the user explicitly overrides - the telemetry logs InstallerHashMismatch with package id, version, channel, and both hashes (L555). MSIX installers get a second path: ReverifyInstallerHash (L641) can validate the package’s SignatureSha256 instead of the whole file’s digest (L659). Only after verification does control reach ExecuteInstaller (InstallFlow.cpp, L489), where ExecuteInstallerForType dispatches per installer family - InstallPackageInstaller (L604) wires the classic handlers. For exe, inno, nullsoft, and burn installers, ShellExecuteInstallImpl (ShellExecuteInstallerHandler.cpp, L326) launches the file through ShellExecuteExW (L38) and watches the spawned process until it exits. Cleanup is explicit too: RemoveInstaller (L722) deletes the temporary installer file when it is no longer needed.

From Index 1.0 to 2.1: build facts straight from the source

  • The catalog index is versioned on disk. src/AppInstallerRepositoryCore/Microsoft/Schema carries interface implementations 1_0 through 1_7 plus 2_0 and 2_1, and version 2.1 adds delta tables (DeltaGeneration.cpp, DeltaTables.cpp) so catalog updates can ship diffs instead of full indexes.
  • The same versioning discipline covers the tool’s other databases: Checkpoint_1_0, Pinning_1_0, and Portable_1_0 live in the same Schema folder, one directory per format.
  • winget resume rests on CheckpointManager.cpp (L18-22), which stores a per-run checkpoints.db under Runtime::PathName::CheckpointsLocation keyed by a CoCreateGuid resume id (L41-45). A failed install leaves its arguments on disk; the resume command replays them.
  • The binary layout is deliberate: the exe is a ten-line shim, and the product ships as WindowsPackageManager.dll, whose Source.def exports both the CLI entry and the server/in-proc initialization functions.
  • Two catalogs, two transports: the winget source is a CDN-hosted SQLite index, msstore is a REST endpoint, and CompositeSource hides the difference from every command (SourceList.cpp, L40-66).

The closest analogues in other ecosystems are formula- and manifest-driven managers. We have taken the same source-level look at Homebrew, the macOS package manager, at pacman on Arch Linux, and at uv, the fast Python package manager - each solves the same manifest-versus-reality problem with different trade-offs.

Honest Limits

  • Every file and line reference here was read from the master tree at the time of writing; C++ refactors move fast, so re-verify before quoting them anywhere important.
  • This tour covered the four core projects. The neighboring surfaces - the Microsoft.Management.Deployment WinRT layer, the PowerShell module, the configuration engine behind winget configure, and the MCP server command - follow the same patterns but were not walked line by line.
  • The hash verification described here is real, but so are its documented override paths and the trust boundary you accept when you add a third-party source; this is a source tour, not a security audit.
  • Search ranking quality, GroupPolicy restrictions, and portable-package behavior each live in their own subsystems and would need their own posts.
entry.summary: Inside microsoft/winget-cli: how the C++ CLI searches its SQLite index, picks installers from YAML manifests, and runs SHA256-verified Windows installs.
